if I lie in any way. I know a certain man of many crafts, a Greek, a Latinist, a mathematician, a philosopher, a physician, and indeed a royal one, now sixty years old. He has cast aside all other matters to twist and torture himself for over twenty years in grammar. He thinks he would be perfectly happy if only he could live long enough to determine with certainty how the eight parts of speech are to be distinguished, something no Greek or Latin writer has yet been able to accomplish fully. It is as if the matter must be settled by war if someone treats a conjunction as belonging to the legal domain of adverbs. And for this reason, since there are as many grammars as there are grammarians—or even more, given that my friend Aldus <note>referring to the printer Aldus Manutius</note> has published his grammar more than five times—this man leaves no book unread, no matter how barbarously or tediously written. He searches and sifts through them all, envious of anyone, no matter how foolishly they labor in this field, miserably fearing that someone might snatch away this glory and that the efforts of so many years might be lost. <summary>Erasmus ridicules an elderly grammarian whose life is consumed by the pedantic and futile pursuit of defining the eight parts of speech.</summary>
